title: Senior Backend Hiring Debrief — Candidate: Omar Haddad
description: The panel debriefs Omar Haddad's onsite loop for the senior backend engineer role and agrees to make an offer.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Okay, let's get started. Thanks everyone for making time, I know it's a packed morning.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: No problem. For context, Omar finished his loop yesterday, so everyone's impressions should still be fresh.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Before we dig in, can we agree on how we're deciding? I'd like each interviewer to give a strong hire, hire, or no hire first, and then we discuss.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: Works for me. Quick reminder of the role: senior backend engineer on the ingestion team, owning the event pipeline roadmap for the next year.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: And we've been looking for this seat since June. That's not a reason to lower the bar, but let's be honest about the cost of waiting.

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: Agreed. I'll go first since I ran the system design round. Strong hire from me.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: Strong hire as well, with one caveat I'll get to.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: I did the values conversation and I'm a hire. Nadia, you?

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Hire. I want to understand the caveats before I go to strong.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: I only met him for thirty minutes at the end, so lean hire, and I'll defer to the people who went deeper.

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: So the prompt was a multi-tenant event ingestion service, roughly fifty thousand events per second at peak, with per-customer rate limits.

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: Omar went straight to failure modes. He asked what happens when one tenant floods us, and proposed partitioning Kafka topics by tenant tier instead of by tenant ID.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: That impressed me too. He called out that hot partitions would be the first thing to bite us, which is exactly what happened to us in the spring.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: Did he talk about backpressure, or just partitioning?

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: Both. He suggested a token bucket at the edge and a dead-letter queue with a replay tool, and he had strong opinions on idempotency keys. An event ID plus a client timestamp bucket.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Was there anything he got wrong?

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: He underestimated storage cost. He guessed about two terabytes a month, and for our largest tenants it's closer to six. But when I gave him the real number, he adjusted the retention tiering on the spot.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: That's the behavior I care about. He revised without getting defensive.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: That matches what I saw. He told me, "I'd rather be corrected early than be wrong in production."

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: He also asked sharp questions about our schema registry, which tells me he has run one before.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: I ran the coding round. He wrote a sliding window rate limiter in Go and finished with fifteen minutes to spare.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: He wrote tests before I asked. His table-driven tests caught an off-by-one in his own window boundary.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: Was it clean code, or interview code?

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: Closer to clean than most. Good naming, and he narrated his thinking without prompting. I'd give communication a nine out of ten.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: How did he handle the follow-up where you changed the requirements?

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: I switched it to a distributed limiter halfway through. He paused, sketched Redis with Lua scripts, and flagged the clock skew problem himself.

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: Same instinct I saw in design. He looks for where things break first.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: One more thing from my side. He was great with the junior folks on the panel. He explained a tradeoff to our intern without talking down to her.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Okay, Imani, you mentioned a caveat.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: Yeah. His last company had about forty engineers and he hasn't managed anyone. The role is senior, not staff, so I want to be sure he isn't expecting a tech lead title in six months.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: I asked him directly. He said he likes mentoring and isn't pushing for management. His goal is staff engineer within three years.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: That's a reasonable timeline, and honestly what I'd hope to hear.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: On compensation, he's at 168 thousand base today and asking for 185. Our senior band tops out at 190.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Did equity come up?

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: He asked about the refresh policy and strike price. He seemed more interested in equity than in the extra base.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: I'd rather stretch equity than base. Can we offer 180 base with a grant above the band midpoint?

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: I can model that. I'll need approval from Fatima since it's above the midpoint.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: I don't love going above midpoint before he's even started, but I'm okay if we tie it to a one-year review.

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: One more concern. He's based in Toronto, and our on-call rotation lands on Pacific hours. He said it was fine, but we should confirm.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Good catch. That deserves a direct question, not an assumption.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: So where are we? Three hires or strong hires, and Tobias at lean hire.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: Lean hire becomes hire. The design round alone convinced me.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Then it's unanimous. Let's make an offer.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: Great. I'll draft the offer letter with 180 base and the larger equity grant, and get Fatima's approval by Thursday.

transcript.speaker: imani
transcript.text: I'll write up the formal scorecard summary and send it to Lucia today, so the approval has a paper trail.

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: I'll call Omar on Friday after the offer goes out. He asked about the team, and a casual chat will help us close.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Can you also confirm the on-call hours with him on that call, Kenji?

transcript.speaker: kenji
transcript.text: Yes, I'll confirm the Pacific on-call timing with him on Friday.

transcript.speaker: tobias
transcript.text: Let's make sure the offer is out by Friday so he doesn't sit on competing offers. He mentioned another process closing next week.

transcript.speaker: lucia
transcript.text: I'll also send Omar a quick thank-you email today so he knows we're moving.

transcript.speaker: me
transcript.text: Perfect. Anything else? No? Thanks, everybody.

summary.overview: The panel debriefed Omar Haddad's onsite loop for the senior backend engineer role. All four interviewers who went deep rated him hire or strong hire, praising his failure-mode thinking in system design, his clean Go code, and how he responded to correction. The open points were seniority expectations, a compensation gap (he asks 185k base against a 190k band cap), and confirming Pacific-hours on-call from Toronto. The group agreed unanimously to make an offer at 180k base with a larger equity grant, targeted to go out by Friday.

notes.title: Kickoff and interview recap
bullets: Four of five interviewers opened with strong hire or hire; Tobias started at lean hire after a short conversation.
Role is senior backend engineer on the ingestion team; the seat has been open since June.

notes.title: System design deep dive
bullets: System design prompt was multi-tenant ingestion at about 50k events per second with per-tenant limits.
Omar proposed partitioning Kafka by tenant tier, a token bucket at the edge, and a dead-letter queue with replay.
He underestimated storage (2 TB vs about 6 TB a month for the largest tenants) but revised retention tiering immediately.

notes.title: Coding round and communication
bullets: Wrote a sliding window rate limiter in Go with 15 minutes to spare and caught his own off-by-one via tests.
Handled a mid-round switch to a distributed limiter by sketching Redis with Lua and flagging clock skew.
Communication rated 9/10; he was also good with the junior panelists.

notes.title: Concerns: seniority and compensation
bullets: No management experience; he wants staff engineer within three years and is not pushing for management.
Currently at 168k base, asking 185k; senior band tops out at 190k and he cares more about equity.
Plan is 180k base with an above-midpoint grant tied to a one-year review, pending Fatima's approval.
Toronto-based, so Pacific on-call hours need to be confirmed directly.

notes.title: Decision and next steps
bullets: Decision is unanimous: make an offer, aiming to send it by Friday because Omar has a competing process closing next week.
Follow-ups are an offer letter, a scorecard write-up, a thank-you email, and a Friday call from Kenji.
